Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- The mother of a woman who gave birth on Monday to octuplets said her daughter already has six children at home and was undergoing fertility treatment. Dr. Karen Maples is part of the large team of doctors and nurses that helped deliver the octuplets. The Los Angeles Times reported on Thursday that Angela Suleman said her daughter had the embryos implanted last year, resulting in the eight births. "They all happened to take," Suleman told the Times. "I looked at those babies. They are so tiny and so beautiful." The woman declined to have the number of embryos reduced when she discovered she was carrying multiples, the Times reported. The six older siblings range from ages 7 to 2, according to the newspaper. Suleman said she was concerned about her daughter's homecoming because her husband, a contract worker, is due to return to Iraq. In the meantime, the mother, who remains unidentified, appealed for privacy while she recovers from giving birth, medical officials said Thursday. In her written statement delivered by Dr. Karen Maples of the Kaiser Permanente Bellflower Medical Center in California, the woman who delivered eight babies in five minutes said she would soon make public the details of her "miraculous experience." "We understand that you are all curious about the arrival of the octuplets, and we appreciate your respect for our family's privacy," she said. "The babies continue to grow strong every day and make good progress. My family and I are ecstatic about all of their arrivals." "Needless to say, the eighth was a surprise to us all, but a blessing as well," she added. The six boys and two girls -- ranging in weight from 1 pound, 8 ounces to 3 pounds, 4 ounces -- are doing well following their Caesarean-section delivery at the Bellflower hospital, doctors said. They were born nine weeks premature. Dr. Mandhir Gupta, a neonatalist, said all but one of the octuplets are now breathing on their own. That baby might be taken off breathing equipment Friday. Caring for eight premature babies is a challenge. Duties are being shared by a large team of hospital nurses and doctors for the time being. Two nurses have been assigned to each child, and all the babies are receiving fluids, proteins and vitamins intravenously, Gupta said. "We feed them. ... We change diapers. ... When they cry, we console them," Gupta said. "When the mom comes and touches the babies, you can definitely see their expression on their faces and body. They are very happy." The babies, who are being referred to by letters of the alphabet, will remain in the hospital for at least seven more weeks. Baby H made headlines for its surprise appearance during the delivery, which took months of preparation by a team of doctors, nurses and respiratory therapists.  Watch a report on babies' progress » . The mother will not be able to hold her babies for another week, Gupta said. They are still fragile, developing intestines, he said. Doctors initially thought the mother was pregnant with seven fetuses. She was hospitalized seven weeks ago and ordered to bed rest. During the seven weeks, a team of 46 physicians, nurses and other staff members prepared for the births. When they started the delivery Monday, they were in for a surprise. "After the seventh baby was born, we were taking a sigh of relief," Maples said. "It was a surprise of our life when we in fact discovered there was an eighth baby," she said. "We never had an assignment for baby H nurse or baby H doctor. We just had to go on the fly and figure out what to do." "Baby G nurse stepped up. We handed off the baby to baby G nurse. She then delivered that last baby to the neonatologist of the baby F." "It was all wonderful because of the teamwork and the training we did before," Maples said.

counterfactuals.output:
# California mother of six gives birth to octuplets after fertility treatment

**LOS ANGELES, California** — A California woman who already had six young children gave birth to octuplets after undergoing fertility treatment, an exceptionally rare delivery that required a large medical team and left all eight premature infants facing weeks of hospital care.

Nadya Suleman, 33, delivered six boys and two girls by Caesarean section January 26, 2009, at Kaiser Permanente Bellflower Medical Center near Los Angeles. The babies were born about nine weeks early and weighed between 1 pound, 8 ounces and 3 pounds, 4 ounces.

Hospital officials said the infants were in stable condition following the delivery. Because of their extreme prematurity and low birth weights, they required intensive monitoring, assistance with breathing and feeding, and were expected to remain hospitalized for several weeks. Some initially needed ventilators, while others were able to breathe with less support.

A team of 46 doctors, nurses and other medical workers participated in the delivery, completing it within minutes.

The births brought Suleman’s number of children to 14. At the time, her six older children were 7, 6, 5, 3 and 2-year-old twins. Suleman, who was unmarried and living with her parents, said all of her children were conceived through in vitro fertilization using sperm from the same donor. One of her older children had autism, and others had developmental needs, according to family statements and media interviews.

Suleman later said six embryos had been transferred during the treatment and that two split, resulting in eight fetuses. The case prompted scrutiny of fertility practices because medical guidelines generally recommend transferring fewer embryos to reduce the risk of dangerous multiple pregnancies.

Multiple births carry significant risks for both the mother and the babies, including premature delivery, low birth weight, breathing problems and long-term developmental complications. Suleman’s doctors said her pregnancy had been closely monitored and that the delivery proceeded without major complications for the mother.

The octuplets were believed to be only the second known set born alive in the United States. Their arrival drew worldwide attention and raised questions about medical ethics, the cost of fertility treatment and the challenges of caring for 14 children.

She initially avoided interviews, saying in a statement: **“I appreciate your respect for my family’s privacy. Please know, in our own time, we will share additional details about this miraculous experience.”** She added, **“The babies continue to grow strong every day and make good progress.”**

- **The babies and delivery:** The octuplets were born about nine weeks prematurely, weighed roughly 1 pound 8 ounces to 3 pounds 4 ounces, and were delivered within about five minutes by a team of 46 medical workers. Doctors had expected seven babies; obstetrician Dr. Harold Henry said, **“We were prepared for seven, and when we saw the eighth, it was a surprise.”** Neonatologist Dr. Mandhir Gupta reported that the infants were **“doing amazingly well,”** while Dr. Karen Maples said, **“They were all screaming and kicking around very vigorously.”**

Why would she do this?”** She also said, **“I’m really tired of taking care of the six children,”** and warned that her daughter **“really, really has no idea what she’s doing to her children and to me.”**

**BREAKING NEWS — Fictional News Report**

# Eight Babies Delivered Nine Weeks Early After Surprise Discovery in Operating Room

**By Staff Correspondent**  
**RIVERTON, Tuesday** — A carefully planned delivery for septuplets became an extraordinary eight-baby birth Tuesday morning when doctors discovered an unexpected eighth child during an emergency cesarean section, hospital officials said.

The six boys and two girls were born at 31 weeks’ gestation—about nine weeks prematurely—at Riverton Regional Medical Center. All eight were admitted immediately to the neonatal intensive care unit, where teams were assisting several of the infants with breathing and closely monitoring their hearts, body temperatures and blood-sugar levels.

Hospital officials said the babies were in serious but stable condition as of Tuesday afternoon. Because premature infants can experience sudden complications, physicians cautioned that the coming days would be critical.

“This was an exceptional delivery, but our attention now is on eight very small patients who each require individualized care,” said Dr. Elena Marquez, the hospital’s chief of maternal-fetal medicine. “They are premature, and they face significant risks, but every baby arrived with a heartbeat and responded to the team’s initial treatment.”

The mother, whose identity was withheld at the family’s request, was recovering in intensive care after the delivery. Doctors described her condition as stable.

## A Planned Operation—and One More Baby

The medical center had spent weeks preparing for the birth after prenatal scans appeared to confirm that the mother was carrying seven babies. She had been admitted for continuous observation because of the high likelihood of premature labor and complications associated with an extremely high-order multiple pregnancy.

Labor began unexpectedly before dawn Tuesday, prompting doctors to proceed with a cesarean section.

One baby after another was delivered and passed through a carefully organized chain of nurses, respiratory therapists and neonatal physicians. Each infant was placed at a numbered resuscitation station with dedicated equipment and personnel.

After the seventh baby was delivered, however, the obstetric team discovered another amniotic sac.

“For a moment, the room became completely still,” said Dr. Marquez. “Then someone said, ‘We have another baby,’ and the entire team moved immediately.”

The eighth infant, a boy, was born less than a minute later. Hospital officials said he had apparently been positioned behind two of his siblings, making him difficult to distinguish during prenatal imaging.

“There was surprise, but there was no panic,” said neonatal director Dr. Marcus Lee. “We had built extra capacity into the plan. That decision proved crucial.”

The infants were delivered over approximately six minutes. The hospital did not immediately release their individual birth weights, but said they ranged from just under 2 pounds to slightly more than 3 pounds.

## Months of Preparation

The operation involved more than 50 medical workers, including obstetricians, anesthesiologists, neonatologists, surgical nurses, respiratory therapists, pharmacists, laboratory technicians and blood-bank personnel.

Hospital administrators had converted two adjacent operating rooms into a combined delivery and stabilization area. Seven neonatal stations were arranged around the rooms, with an eighth reserve station positioned nearby in case equipment failed or an additional infant required emergency treatment.

Each station contained a warming bed, oxygen equipment, breathing tubes, monitors, medication and supplies sized for extremely small newborns. Teams rehearsed the delivery repeatedly, assigning each expected baby a color and number so staff members could track treatment without confusion.

The hospital also secured additional incubators, alerted nearby medical centers and placed extra units of blood on standby for the mother.

“We rehearsed how the babies would be handed off, where each team would stand and even how people would move through the doors,” said charge nurse Angela Foster. “With this many infants, organization is not optional. Every second and every step matter.”

The hospital had initially assigned one neonatal team to each of the seven babies doctors expected. An additional emergency group—including a neonatologist, two nurses and a respiratory therapist—was kept outside the operating room as backup.

That group took charge of the eighth baby.

“It was exactly the kind of contingency we hoped we would never need,” Foster said. “But when we needed it, they were ready.”

## Long NICU Stay Expected

Several of the newborns were placed on ventilators, while others received less invasive breathing support. Doctors said premature babies born at 31 weeks often need help maintaining body temperature, feeding and fighting infection.

The infants are expected to remain in the neonatal intensive care unit for several weeks, possibly until near their original due date. Physicians said they would watch for complications including bleeding in the brain, intestinal disease, infection and problems involving the lungs and eyes.

The babies will initially receive nutrition intravenously. Small amounts of milk may be introduced through feeding tubes as their conditions allow.

Dr. Lee emphasized that the infants’ shared birth did not mean their medical progress would be identical.

“People naturally think of them as a group of eight, but medically they are eight individual patients,” he said. “One may need a ventilator longer. Another may begin feeding sooner. Their treatment plans will change hour by hour.”

## Family Requests Privacy

In a brief statement released by the hospital, the parents thanked the medical team and asked for privacy.

“We are overwhelmed, grateful and still trying to understand that we are now the parents of eight newborns,” the statement said. “We thank the doctors and nurses who prepared so carefully and who are caring for our children.”

Relatives who gathered at the hospital said the family had prepared for seven babies by assembling donated cribs, clothing and car seats. News of the eighth brought a mixture of disbelief and joy.

Hospital officials said social workers and community organizations were already discussing long-term support for the family, including transportation, housing adjustments, infant supplies and specialized medical follow-up.

The medical center plans to provide another update Wednesday, but doctors said detailed information would be limited to protect the family’s privacy.

“This is an uplifting moment, but it is also the beginning of a long and uncertain medical journey,” Dr. Marquez said. “Today’s achievement belongs to the mother, the babies and a team that prepared for every possibility—including, as it turned out, one possibility more than we expected.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
